title: Hedging and impersonal structures
tagline: Say it without overclaiming it: impersonal subjects and softened verbs do the distancing for you.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (it, there, one, seems, appears)
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (arguably, presumably, tend to, one)
Writing Part 1 — essay: arguing a case without overclaiming
Speaking Parts 3 and 4 — softening an opinion without sounding vague
why: Hedging is how careful C1-level writers avoid sounding more certain than the evidence allows — 'the data suggest' rather than 'the data prove'. English has a whole toolkit for this: impersonal subjects like 'it' and 'there', the generic pronoun 'one', and the agentless passive all remove the person making the claim and turn it into a careful observation. C1 Advanced rewards this in the essay, where a confident-but-hedged argument scores higher than an overstated one, and tests the vocabulary of tentativeness directly in Use of English.

items: the passive: it is believed that

head: Device
Function
Example
rows: it seems / appears that
softens an observation based on present evidence
It appears that the new timetable has reduced absences.
it would seem that
extra distance — more tentative than 'seems'
It would seem that the plan was never realistic.
tend to
a general pattern, not an absolute rule
Younger students tend to underestimate how long revision takes.
arguably / presumably / apparently
an adverb that hedges a whole sentence
Arguably, the exam was too long for the time given.
there is some evidence that
impersonal, cites unnamed evidence
There is some evidence that shorter lessons improve focus.
may / might / could + verb
a modal for tentative possibility
The results may reflect a change in teaching method.
one
a generic subject, distances the writer from 'I'
One could argue that the reform came too late.
passive without an agent
removes the person making the claim
It is widely believed that the merger will go ahead.

use.point: Softening a claim with impersonal it/there + a verb of appearance

examples.text: It appears that the new policy has had little real effect.
It would seem that the committee underestimated the cost.
There is some evidence that students learn better in smaller groups.
Arguably, the school could have consulted parents earlier.
examples.note: the adverb hedges the whole sentence

examples.text: Younger candidates tend to rush the final section of the exam.
examples.note: 'tend to' describes a general pattern, not every single case

examples.text: The results were, presumably, affected by the change of venue.
examples.note: presumably = the writer is guessing based on reason, not certainty

examples.text: This drop in attendance may reflect the new bus schedule, rather than a loss of interest.
examples.note: may + verb: one possible explanation among others

examples.text: The delay could well be connected to the recent staff changes.
examples.note: 'could well' is a natural, plausible hedge

examples.text: Further research might reveal other contributing factors.
examples.note: might = a weaker possibility than may

examples.text: One might question whether the deadline was realistic in the first place.
examples.note: formal 'one' replaces 'I' for a generalised opinion

examples.text: It is generally accepted that exam stress affects performance.
examples.note: agentless passive — no one is named as accepting it

examples.text: The proposal is thought to have been rejected for budgetary reasons.
examples.note: passive + infinitive, hedges without naming who thinks it

watch_out.wrong: It seem that the plan will not work.
watch_out.right: It seems that the plan will not work.
watch_out.why: 'It' is singular, so the verb needs an -s: it seems, not it seem.

watch_out.wrong: Presumably that the results were affected by the weather.
watch_out.right: Presumably, the results were affected by the weather.
watch_out.why: Sentence adverbs like presumably/arguably/apparently stand alone — they don't take 'that' the way a verb like 'seem' does.

watch_out.wrong: Students tend rushing the last question.
watch_out.right: Students tend to rush the last question.
watch_out.why: 'Tend to' is followed by the to-infinitive, not the -ing form.

watch_out.wrong: One should be careful with his conclusions.
watch_out.why: Formal 'one' keeps its own possessive form, 'one's', rather than switching to 'his' or 'their'.

watch_out.wrong: It is believe that the reform will be delayed.
watch_out.right: It is believed that the reform will be delayed.
watch_out.why: The impersonal passive needs the past participle after 'is/are': is believed, not is believe.

watch_out.wrong: The results could may show a wider pattern.
watch_out.right: The results could show a wider pattern.
watch_out.why: Only one modal per verb phrase — never stack two modals like 'could may'.

dialogue.title: Presenting the survey results
dialogue.context: Nadia, Mateo and Sofia are preparing the results of their class survey on study habits for a presentation, and Miss Vega reminds them not to claim more than the data actually show.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: You surveyed forty students, not the whole school, so be careful with how you word your conclusions.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: So I shouldn't write 'Students don't revise enough'?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Exactly — try something more careful: 'It appears that many students underestimate how much revision they need.'

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: What about the result on phone use? Nearly everyone who scored low said they revised with their phone nearby.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good — you can hedge that with a modal: 'Low scores may be linked to phone use during revision.'

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: There is some evidence that students who study in silence remember more, but our sample is small.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Perfect phrasing. And instead of saying 'I think group study doesn't work', try distancing yourself a little.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: 'Arguably, group study is less effective for exam revision, although some students clearly prefer it.'

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: One could also argue that motivation matters more than method.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Nice. And for the final slide?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: 'It is widely believed that shorter, more frequent revision sessions work better than long ones — our results would seem to support that.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: That's exactly the tone a C1 presentation needs — confident, but never overstating the evidence.

items.sentence: ___ that the new bus route has reduced congestion near the school.
items.why: impersonal 'it' takes a singular verb: it appears, followed by a that-clause

items.sentence: The committee's decision, ___, was influenced by budget concerns.
items.why: the sentence adverb 'presumably' hedges the whole clause

items.sentence: Younger students ___ underestimate how long an essay takes to plan.
items.why: 'tend to' + bare infinitive expresses a general pattern

items.sentence: The delay ___ be connected to last week's staff changes.
items.why: 'could well' is a natural hedge meaning 'quite possibly'

items.sentence: ___ might question whether the survey sample was large enough.
items.why: generic 'one' gives a formal, impersonal tone rather than a personal opinion

items.sentence: It ___ believed that the results reflect a wider national trend.
items.why: the impersonal passive agrees with 'it': it is believed

items.sentence: There ___ some evidence that shorter lessons improve concentration.
items.why: 'there is' agrees with the uncountable noun 'evidence'

items.sentence: The results ___ a wider pattern, though more research is needed.
items.why: only one modal per verb phrase: could show, not could may show

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one or two words.

items.sentence: It ___ (seem) that the new timetable has helped attendance.
___, the delay was caused by the printer breaking down twice.
Students who revise in short bursts ___ to remember more in the long run.
The drop in sales ___ well be linked to the new pricing policy.
___ could argue that the deadline was unrealistic from the start.
It is widely ___ that the museum will reopen by December.
There ___ some evidence that smaller classes improve results.
The results ___ reflect a broader trend, though the sample is small.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: The department could have planned the trip better.
The reform will probably be delayed because of the budget cuts.
Younger students usually underestimate how long revision takes.
It's possible that the delay is connected to staff changes.
People generally believe that the museum will reopen in December.
items.second_end: that the museum will reopen in December.

items.first: I think the deadline was unrealistic.
items.second_end: argue that the deadline was unrealistic.

summary: Use impersonal it + a verb of appearance (seems, appears, would seem) + a that-clause to present a claim as an observation, not a fact.
Adverbs like arguably, presumably, apparently hedge a whole sentence and stand alone — they don't take 'that' the way 'seem' does.
Modals (may, might, could) and phrases like tend to soften a claim into one possible explanation among others.
Generic one and the agentless passive (it is believed that) remove the person making the claim for a formal, academic tone.
In speech, the same idea sounds looser: sort of, kind of, I'd say — keep these out of formal writing.
